analysis.one_liner: Requires firearms to carry a label with the national suicide prevention hotline number.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell a gun unless the gun or its packaging carries a clear label, in English and Spanish, giving the toll-free number for the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, with a warning triangle like other consumer warnings. It would be enforced under existing consumer product safety penalty rules and would take effect two years after passage. It was introduced in September 2023 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People in suicidal crisis and their families. Firearms are used in roughly half of suicides in the United States, and a hotline label on the weapon or its packaging is a low-cost attempt to put help in front of someone at the moment of highest risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in suicidal crisis and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits manufacturers and retailers, including licensed dealers, from selling any firearm that does not carry a clear and conspicuous label with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline's toll-free number, in English and Spanish, on the gun, its packaging, or its descriptive material [S3].
The label must include a yellow warning triangle with an exclamation mark, mirroring the warning format used for other hazardous consumer products [S3].

Violations would be treated as violations of the Consumer Product Safety Act and subject to its civil and criminal penalties, giving the requirement actual enforcement teeth rather than relying on voluntary industry action [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and licensed dealers, who would bear the cost of printing and attaching labels within two years of enactment, and who lose the ability to sell unlabeled firearms.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own mechanism is modest: a label does not restrict access to firearms or require safe storage, so its supporters can only claim it may reach someone at the moment of crisis, not that it prevents deaths on its own [S3].

The bill overrides the statutory exclusion that keeps firearms outside the Consumer Product Safety Act's definition of a consumer product, meaning it would subject firearms to consumer-product-style regulation and penalties — a change gun manufacturers and dealers would treat as a costly precedent and a compliance burden [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but limited: a hotline label costs manufacturers and dealers very little and could reach a person in crisis at a moment when a phone number matters. The cost side is compliance and, more important to the industry, the precedent of treating guns as regulable consumer products. On balance this is a low-cost safety measure, but it is a small step rather than a comprehensive suicide-prevention policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever took it up; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Julia Brownley introduced the Gun Suicide Prevention Act on September 14, 2023, with four original cosponsors: Representatives Moulton, Napolitano, Grijalva, and Tlaib [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it remained [S5].
Twenty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and no vote on it was ever taken in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and dealers are better off: they never had to label firearms, and the precedent of consumer-product-style regulation of guns never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats out of 216 House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted; no Republican supported the bill on the record.

industries.note: The bill would require a suicide hotline label on every gun sold and enforce it with consumer-product penalties, a modest compliance cost. The industry's interest in avoiding any consumer-product-style regulation of firearms runs against the labeling's purpose of reaching people in suicidal crisis.
